about: The Vulcan course plan. Units teach 3-6 new items each, words before phrases before sentences. Every Vulcan form is a {key} template rendered from lexicon/lexicon.csv by tools/build_course.py, so the course always matches the dictionary. Item ids are derived from the template, so progress survives reordering units. 'errors' are spot-the-mistake drills: the right template, one or more wrong ones, and why.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.about: Greetings, people, description, basic sentences, questions, evidentials, honorifics and naming feelings. From lessons 1 to 8.

levels.title: Conversation
levels.about: Living among others: receiving a guest, confiding, the training hall and the deep desert, then life between bondmates: homecoming, comfort in the night, mending a quarrel, the private name and parting. Built from the Phrasebook scenes.

levels.title: Literary and Ceremonial
levels.about: Vulcan tales and how they are told, sayings that compress them, then the Teachings, ceremonial Vulcan, emotive and Classical forms, and reading fiction.

levels.title: Academy
levels.about: Science Academy prose: the formal register, technical and philosophical vocabulary, argument and citation.

units.title: Greetings
units.tip: A formal greeting has a fixed reply. Answer t'nar with t'nar jaral, and the blessing with peace and long life.

items.en: Greetings; I extend regard to your house.

errors.en: The reply to "live long and prosper"
errors.why: Echoing the blessing back is a human habit. The formal reply is peace and long life.

units.title: Courtesy
units.tip: Yes and no stand at the front, then the courtesy word.

units.title: Please
units.tip: Please comes first and the verb comes last. Everything else sits between them.

errors.why: Please opens the request and the verb closes it.

units.title: This one, that one
units.tip: Vulcans say "this one" for I and "that one" for he or she. Identity uses wim, with -ish for I.

units.title: Names
units.tip: The possessor follows the noun: name my, name your.

errors.why: The possessor follows the noun, and a description needs no verb.

units.title: Good and bad
units.tip: No verb "to be" in a description: "this good" means "this is good."

units.title: The house
units.tip: Noun, then adjective, then possessor: house old my is "my old house."

errors.why: As a phrase, the adjective comes right after the noun and the possessor last. House my old would be a sentence: "my house is old."

units.title: Seeing and wanting
units.tip: Subject, object, verb. A definite object takes -wizh.

errors.why: The verb comes last, and -wizh attaches to the object, never the verb.

units.title: Eating and drinking
units.tip: -pil on the verb means it is happening now: "is drinking."

units.title: Coming and going
units.tip: -un marks the past. Dungi before the verb marks the future. -fi means toward.

errors.why: Dungi stands right before the verb. -un is the past, not the future.

units.title: Asking
units.tip: Question words go first. A yes-or-no question opens with kuth. Answer by repeating the verb.

errors.why: Kuth opens a yes-or-no question.

units.title: How you know
units.tip: An evidential ends the sentence: ho if you saw it, aukh if you concluded it, k'en if you were told.

items.en: The ship came here. (I saw it.)

errors.why: The evidential ends the sentence, and it must match how you know: told is k'en, seen is ho.

units.title: Comparing
units.tip: X, then Y t'ei, then li (more) or osh (less), then the quality.

errors.why: T'ei follows the thing being compared against, as in Japanese kore wa are yori: "this, that-than."

units.title: Counting
units.tip: Numbers follow the noun, and they are regular: ten-one is eleven, two-ten is twenty.

units.title: Building words
units.tip: Learn the pieces and the vocabulary multiplies: -ve is the person, -puhl the place, -uth the act.

units.title: Speaking up, speaking down
units.tip: Raise the other with -mush or cheil; lower yourself with -fum. Between t'hy'la, use none of it.

errors.why: Between t'hy'la, plain speech is itself the honor. Formal endings and honored address put distance where there should be none.

units.title: Naming a feeling
units.tip: A Vulcan does not say "I am afraid." They say "fear is in me," and close with kon: noted.

items.en: There is fear in me. Noted.

errors.en: There is fear in me. Noted.
errors.why: Standard Vulcan never makes the self the one who feels. The feeling is in you, observed and noted.
Another person's feeling is never stated bare. You can only conclude it, so it takes aukh.

units.title: Asking leave
units.tip: A Vulcan asks leave before any touch, even of a child.

items.en: There is joy in me. Noted.

units.title: Receiving a guest
units.tip: In the desert, water comes before any word. A host who does not offer it has insulted the guest.

items.en: the water-first: water offered before any word
a favor, a debt of kindness
Please sit. Let us share names.
Your House's reputation is great, I am told.

errors.en: Your House's reputation is great, I am told.
errors.why: A reputation is hearsay, so it takes k'en. The possessor follows what it owns: the House is yours.

units.title: The heart-whisper
units.tip: A heart-whisper may be told only to bond-kin. Told to anyone else, the same words are rumor.

items.en: confide a heart-matter about someone absent
There is attraction in me. Noted.
There is attraction in her too, I conclude.

errors.en: There is attraction in her, I conclude.
errors.why: Another person's feeling is never stated bare. You concluded it from what you saw, so aukh. Tekh would mean you had touched her mind.

units.title: The training hall
units.tip: Students rank by when they began. A junior asking leave puts kup first and lowers themself with -fum.

errors.why: A junior asking the master lowers themself with -fum, and kup, "may," comes first in a request for leave.

units.title: Lost in the desert
units.from: Phrasebook scene: lost in the deep desert
units.tip: Say how you know: a storm read from the wind is aukh, a cave you can see is ho.

items.en: No. A sandstorm is coming, I conclude.

errors.en: There, a cave. I see it.
errors.why: You can see the cave, so ho. Aukh is for what you conclude, k'en for what you were told.
One negative per clause: nothing already carries it.

units.title: Coming home
units.tip: Standard Vulcans report what the bond feels, as evidence with tekh, instead of displaying a feeling. "The bond-silence was long" means "I missed you."

items.en: bond-silence: where a bonded mind is no longer felt
bond-warmth: a bondmate felt through the bond
bond-ache: the pain of long distance
reach for someone through the bond
The bond-silence was long. (I missed you.)
I missed you. (There was missing in me. Noted.)
Now there is warmth. I feel it through the bond.

errors.en: Now there is warmth. I feel it through the bond.
errors.why: The bond is felt, not seen or heard about: tekh, the evidential of touch and the bond.

units.title: In the night
units.tip: Even between bondmates, a Vulcan asks leave before touching. Name the fear, then state the fact.

items.en: a comforting touch, given with leave
There is fear in you. Noted. You are safe.

errors.en: There is fear in you. Noted.
errors.why: Calling someone fearful labels them. Standard names the feeling as present in them, with tok before the one who feels it and kon at the end.

units.title: Mending a quarrel
units.tip: Apologize with -fum. Offering the hand ends the quarrel, because holding hands is intimate among Vulcans.

errors.why: The possessor follows the noun, and -wizh goes on the last word of the object phrase.

units.title: The private name
units.tip: A bondmate's private name is the given name with -pi. Standard says "I hold you in regard"; Classical says "I cherish you." Both mean I love you.

items.en: private name, used only by a bondmate

errors.en: I hold you in regard. (I love you.)
errors.why: Subject, object, verb, and the one held in regard carries -wizh. The last one says "you hold me in regard."

units.title: Before a parting
units.tip: Time comes first in the sentence, and the future marker dungi sits right before the verb.

items.en: Far from home, near in the bond.

errors.why: Dungi sits directly before the verb, after the object.

units.title: Telling a tale
units.tip: A tale opens with k'en, because the teller did not see it happen, and ends with a question. The listener draws the lesson, with aukh.

items.en: the sehlat who ate its tail

errors.why: A tale is reported, not seen or worked out. The teller opens with k'en and does not vouch for it.

errors.en: the sehlat who ate its tail
errors.why: Lith follows the noun it describes, and the relative clause keeps subject-object-verb order.

units.title: Journeys and trials
units.tip: Long tales are sung in verses, a few each night. Falor's Journey has 348, and every verse closes on the refrain.

items.en: He looked at his fear, and set it aside.

errors.why: The refrain is in the ongoing present, -pil, so each night the journey is still going on. -un would end it.

stories.title: The ambassador
stories.setting: A Vulcan ambassador meets a Starfleet officer who is still learning.

lines.en: Greetings; I extend regard to your house.
Greetings, likewise. Do you speak Vulcan?
Yes. You speak it, I observe.
I am learning. Please speak slowly.
How goes your work?
My work goes well, thank you.
Would you like tea?
Yes, thank you.

questions.q: How does the ambassador know the officer speaks Vulcan?
questions.right: She concludes it from hearing her (aukh)

questions.q: What does the ambassador ask about instead of "how are you"?
What does the officer accept?

stories.title: A family supper
stories.setting: Supper at home. Short sentences, subjects dropped.

lines.en: The meal is ready. Please sit.
The soup is hot. Eat slowly.
I am hungry.
Please pour the tea.
Did you go to school today?
Yes. The teacher taught a new lesson.
What lesson?
Astronomy. The great sun is hotter than all.
Fascinating.

questions.q: Why does the mother tell her son to eat slowly?
What did the son learn today?
"Nash-ve tuhkukhuk" states hunger plainly. Why is that acceptable in Standard Vulcan?
questions.right: Hunger is a bodily state, not an emotional display
wrong: Children are allowed to show feelings
It is said in the humble register

stories.title: The briefing
stories.setting: On the bridge of a Vulcan ship. Every report says how the speaker knows.

lines.en: What did the sensors see?
A new ship is coming here. Observed.
Is it dangerous?
Perhaps. It has weapons, I conclude.
Activate the shields.
Understood. When will it arrive?
Soon.
Send a signal: greetings, I extend regard to your house.
The signal has been sent.
Logical.

questions.q: The science officer says the ship has weapons. How does she know?
questions.right: She concludes it from the readings (aukh)
wrong: She saw the weapons on her instruments (ho)

questions.q: What does the captain do before sending a greeting?
Which greeting goes out in the signal?

stories.title: A family lesson
stories.setting: A child speaks the old way. Her grandmother teaches the Standard one.

lines.en: I'm furious!
No. There is anger in you. Say "noted."
There is anger in me. Noted.
Good. Why?
My younger sibling taunted me.
Taunting is illogical. But rage is illogical too.
I forgive my younger sibling.
May this one touch you?
You have leave.
Now there is calm in you. I know it by touch.

questions.q: What is wrong with the child's first sentence, by Standard rules?
questions.right: She makes herself the one who feels instead of naming the feeling

questions.q: Why does the grandmother ask leave before touching her own grandchild?
questions.right: Leave is asked before any touch, even of a child
wrong: She is a stranger to the child

questions.q: How does the grandmother know the child is calm?

stories.title: The water-first
stories.setting: A Starfleet officer visits a desert household in the Forge.

lines.en: Welcome. Take water.
Thank you. I have brought a guest-gift.
Please sit. Let us share names.
My name is Hana. I am Human.
My name is Sorek. My House is Suvek.
You speak Vulcan, I observe.
I am learning.
Water shared is life shared.

questions.q: What does the host offer before anything else?
What has the officer brought?
What does "let us share names" begin?

stories.title: The heart-keeper
stories.setting: Two t'hy'la, late in the evening. Sorel has something to confide.

lines.en: There is attraction in me. Noted.
Toward whom?
Toward T'Lara.
Does she know?
No. I have not told her.
She watches you. I have seen it.
There is attraction in her too, I conclude.
Please keep the confidence.
I will keep it.

questions.q: How does Taren know T'Lara watches Sorel?
Has Sorel told T'Lara?
wrong: He asked Taren to tell her

questions.q: Why may Sorel tell this to Taren?
questions.right: Taren is bond-kin; told to anyone else it would be rumor

stories.title: The storm
stories.setting: A guide and a traveler, two days into a desert crossing that has gone wrong.

lines.en: Two water-skins remain.
Is the oasis near?
No. A sandstorm is coming, I conclude.
Ration the water.
Where is shelter?
There, a cave. I see it.
Light a night-fire. A signal fire too.
I am thirsty.
The desert forgives nothing. Drink slowly.

questions.q: How does the guide know a storm is coming?
questions.right: He concludes it, from the wind (aukh)

questions.q: Where do they shelter?
Why light a second fire?

stories.title: Come back
stories.setting: T'Rena leaves on a long mission. Sorel sees her off, and months later she returns.

lines.en: Tomorrow I go.
I carry worry for you.
Please set the worry aside.
Return safely.
Take my keepsake.
I will wait for you.
You have returned.
I have. The bond-silence was long.
I missed you. (There was missing in me. Noted.)
Now there is warmth. I feel it through the bond.
Let us share silence.

questions.q: What does T'Rena give Sorel before she leaves?
What is T'Rena telling Sorel when she says the bond-silence was long?
wrong: She chose not to reach for him

questions.q: How does T'Rena know there is warmth now?

stories.title: The sehlat who ate its tail
stories.setting: A teaching tale for small children, told to explain the saying Spock uses in SNW "The Sehlat Who Ate Its Tail."

lines.en: Long ago, it is told, there lived a young sehlat.
Every day the sehlat saw its own tail.
The sehlat thought that the tail was food.
The sehlat chased the tail: one day, two days, three days.
It did not eat. It did not drink. It did not rest.
An elder asked the sehlat: "Why are you chasing it?"
"I am hungry. Food is near. I see it."
On the fourth day, the sehlat caught its tail.
It bit the tail. The pain was great.
The sehlat sat down. Its tail was short. Its stomach was empty.
"You hunted yourself."
The tale ends. What do you conclude?
The sehlat saw its tail, but did not understand what it saw. I conclude.

questions.q: Why does the sehlat say food is near?
questions.right: It saw its own tail (ho) and took it for food
wrong: It smelled prey on the wind

questions.q: What did the sehlat hunt, in the end?
Who says what the tale means?
questions.right: The listener, by drawing a conclusion with aukh

stories.title: Falor's Journey
stories.setting: A parent sings the opening verses of Falor's Journey, a tale of enlightenment in 348 verses, the tale Tuvok sings to frightened children in VOY "Innocence". A few verses are sung each night, closing with the night verse.

lines.en: Falor left his home. The path was long, the night was long. Falor walks on.
Falor crossed the desert. The sand was hot, the water-skin empty. Falor walks on.
Falor climbed the mountain. The wind was cold, the stars near. Falor walks on.
Falor met his fear. He looked at it, and set it aside. Falor walks on.
Falor asked a teacher: "Where is truth?" The teacher answered: "Walk." Falor walks on.
Night has come. Rest, little one. Falor will walk tomorrow.
Falor returned home. The home was the same; Falor was not. The journey ends.

questions.q: What does Falor do after every trial?
What does Falor do with his fear?
questions.right: He looks at it and sets it aside

questions.q: In the last verse, what has changed?

stories.title: The kahs-wan
stories.setting: A teaching tale told to children before their own kahs-wan, the maturity ordeal in the desert that young Spock faces in TAS "Yesteryear."

lines.en: Long ago, it is told, a child went out for the kahs-wan.
She carried one water-skin. The kahs-wan is faced alone.
On the third day, she found a wounded stranger.
"I am thirsty."
The child looked at her water-skin. The water was not enough.
But she gave water to the stranger.
The stranger taught her water-finding.
On the seventh day, the stranger died. The child built a cairn.
On the tenth day, she returned home.
"Did you survive alone?"
"No. I shared my water. The stranger taught me water-finding."
"Your kahs-wan is complete."
The tale ends. What do you conclude?
Water shared is life shared. I conclude.

questions.q: What did the child give the stranger?
What did the stranger give her in return?
Why do the elders call her kahs-wan complete, though she was not alone?
questions.right: She kept the desert way: water shared is life shared
wrong: She came back on the tenth day
